description: Proofs involving Big O, Omega, and Theta notation

blocks.latex: \text{To show } f(n) = \Theta(g(n)) \text{, we need to show } f(n) = O(g(n)) \text{ and } f(n) = \Omega(g(n)).
f(n) = {{complexity:O}}(g(n)) \text{ if there exist positive constants } c_1 \text{ and } n_0 \text{ such that } 0 {{op:\leq}} f(n) {{op:\leq}} c_1g(n) \text{ for all } n {{op:\geq}} n_0.
f(n) = {{complexity:\Omega}}(g(n)) \text{ if there exist positive constants } c_2 \text{ and } n_0 \text{ such that } 0 {{op:\leq}} c_2g(n) {{op:\leq}} f(n) \text{ for all } n {{op:\geq}} n_0.
\text{Apply these definitions with } f(n) = n^2 + n^3 \text{ and } g(n) = n^3.
\text{For O-notation: } n^2 + n^3 {{op:\leq}} n^3 + n^3 \text{ (for } n {{op:\geq}} 1 \text{)}
\text{So, } c_1 = 2, n_0 = 1 \text{ satisfies } n^2 + n^3 \le c_1n^3.
\text{For } \Omega \text{-notation: We need } c_2n^3 \le n^2 + n^3.
\text{Since } n^2 \ge 0 \text{, then } n^3 \le n^2 + n^3 \text{ for } n \ge 1 \text{.}
\text{So, } c_2 = 1, n_0 = 1 \text{ satisfies } c_2n^3 \le n^2 + n^3.
\text{Therefore, } n^2 + n^3 = {{complexity:\Theta}}(n^3).

\text{To show } f(n) = {{complexity:O}}(g(n)) \text{, we need to find positive constants } c \text{ and } n_0 \text{ such that } 0 {{op:\leq}} f(n) {{op:\leq}} cg(n) \text{ for all } n {{op:\geq}} n_0.
\text{Apply this with } f(n) = \log_2 n \text{ and } g(n) = n \text{ (the base of the logarithm only changes the constant).}
\text{By induction on } n \text{, we have } n < 2^n \text{ for all } n {{op:\geq}} 1 \text{ (doubling adds at least 1 each step).}
\text{Taking } \log_2 \text{ of both sides of } n < 2^n \text{ gives } \log_2 n {{op:\leq|<}} n.
\text{Therefore, } \log_2 n \le 1 \cdot n \text{ for all } n \ge 1.
\text{So, } c = 1 \text{ and } n_0 = 1 \text{ satisfy the definition.}
\text{Therefore, } \log n = O(n).
\text{To show } f(n) = O(g(n)) \text{, we need to find positive constants } c \text{ and } n_0 \text{ such that } 0 \le f(n) \le cg(n) \text{ for all } n \ge n_0.
\text{Apply this with } f(n) = n \log n \text{ (logarithm base 2) and } g(n) = n^2.
\text{We need to show that } n \log n \le c \cdot n^2 \text{ for some constants } c \text{ and } n_0.
\text{Dividing both sides by } n \text{ (assuming } n > 0 \text{): } \log n \le c \cdot n.
\text{We know that } \log n < n \text{ for all } n \ge 1.
\text{Therefore, } \log n \le 1 \cdot n \text{ for all } n \ge 1.
\text{Multiplying both sides by } n: n \log n \le n^2 \text{ for all } n \ge 1.
\text{So, } c = 1 \text{ and } n_0 = 1 \text{ satisfy the definition.}
\text{Therefore, } n \log n = O(n^2).
\text{To show } f(n) \neq O(g(n)) \text{, we need to show that} \text{ for any positive constants } c \text{ and } n_0 \text{, there exists } n \ge n_0 \text{ such that } f(n) > cg(n).
\text{Apply this with } f(n) = 2^n \text{ and } g(n) = n^3 \text{ (logarithms below are base 2).}
\text{Assume for contradiction that } 2^n = O(n^3) \text{, so } 2^n \le c \cdot n^3 \text{ for some } c > 0 \text{ and all } n \ge n_0.
\text{Taking logarithms: } n \le \log(c \cdot n^3) = \log c + 3 \log n.
\text{Rearranging: } n - 3 \log n \le \log c.
\text{But } \lim_{n \to \infty} (n - 3 \log n) = \infty \text{ since } n \text{ grows faster than } \log n.
\text{This means } n - 3 \log n \text{ can be arbitrarily large, contradicting } n - 3 \log n \le \log c.
\text{Therefore, our assumption is false, and } 2^n \neq O(n^3).

puzzles.title: \text{Prove: if } f(n) = O(g(n)) \text{ and } g(n) = O(h(n)) \text{, then } f(n) = O(h(n))
puzzles.statement: f(n) = O(g(n)) \text{ and } g(n) = O(h(n)) \implies f(n) = O(h(n))

blocks.latex: \text{Since } f(n) = O(g(n)) \text{, there are constants } c_1 > 0 \text{ and } n_1 \text{ with } 0 \le f(n) \le c_1 g(n) \text{ for all } n \ge n_1.
\text{Similarly, since } g(n) = O(h(n)) \text{, there are } c_2 > 0 \text{ and } n_2 \text{ with } 0 \le g(n) \le c_2 h(n) \text{ for all } n \ge n_2.
\text{Let } n_0 = \max(n_1, n_2) \text{, so both bounds hold for all } n \ge n_0.
\text{For } n \ge n_0 \text{: } f(n) {{op:\leq}} c_1 g(n) {{op:\leq}} c_1 c_2 h(n) \text{, multiplying the second bound by } c_1 > 0.
\text{So with } c = c_1 c_2 > 0 \text{, we have } 0 \le f(n) \le c \cdot h(n) \text{ for all } n \ge n_0.
\text{Therefore } f(n) = {{complexity:O}}(h(n)).

puzzles.title: \text{Prove: } T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n \text{ is } O(n \log n)
puzzles.displayTitle: Prove: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n is O(n log n)
puzzles.statement: T(1) = 1 \text{ and } T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n \text{ for powers of two } n \ge 2 \text{. Show } T(n) = O(n \log_2 n).

blocks.latex: \text{Claim: } T(n) = n \log_2 n + n \text{ for every power of two } n \ge 1 \text{. We prove it by induction on } n.
\textbf{Base case: } T(1) = 1 = 1 \cdot \log_2 1 + 1 \text{, since } \log_2 1 = 0.
\textbf{Inductive step: } \text{assume } T(n/2) = \tfrac{n}{2} \log_2 \tfrac{n}{2} + \tfrac{n}{2} \text{ for a power of two } n \ge 2.
T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n = 2\left(\tfrac{n}{2} \log_2 \tfrac{n}{2} + \tfrac{n}{2}\right) + n
= n \log_2 \tfrac{n}{2} + n + n
= n(\log_2 n - 1) + 2n \text{, since } \log_2 \tfrac{n}{2} = \log_2 n - 1
= n \log_2 n + n \text{, which completes the induction.}
\text{For } n {{op:\geq}} 2 \text{ we have } \log_2 n \ge 1 \text{, so } n \le n \log_2 n.
\text{Hence } T(n) = n \log_2 n + n {{op:\leq}} 2n \log_2 n \text{ for all } n \ge 2.
\text{With } c = 2 \text{ and } n_0 = 2 \text{, } T(n) = {{complexity:O}}(n \log n).
